text.p: History repeated itself at the $4.45 million Lipton Championships on Saturday when Boris Becker withdrew from the tournament for the third time and defending champion Andre Agassi was beaten in his first match.

Agassi, the 12th seed, looked occasionally sharp but mostly mediocre, and was defeated by hard-serving Australian lefthander, Scott Draper, 7-6 (7-5) 6-1. It was his fourth first-match defeat this year.

Becker, seeded 10th, withdrew from the tournament just two hours before his first match with fellow German, Hendrik Dreekman. A nagging wrist injury, sustained at Wimbledon, forced Becker's departure. It was the third time Becker had withdrawn since the tournament began in 1985. Both Becker and Agassi had first-round byes.
Top seed Pete Sampras provided a study in contrasts by demolishing Romania's Adrian Voinea 6-2 6-0.

Britain's bright star, Tim Henman, went down in flames just three days after receiving the ATP Tour's award as the Most Improved Player in 1996. Henman, seeded 14th, was beaten by little-known Spanish qualifier Julian Alonso, 6-7 (4-7) 6-2 6-3.
Henman is ranked 16. Alonso, who had never won a match in the main draw of an ATP Tour event prior to this week, is ranked 228.

In women's second round play, 12th-seeded Amanda Coetzer of South Africa was upset 6-1 3-6 6-3 by Russian teen phenomenon Anna Kournikova, 15 years old and ranked 90. Another Russian teenager, 19-year old Tatiana Panova, beat Brenda Schultz McCarthy, the 15th seed from the Netherlands, 1-6 7-6(7-2) 6-4.

Agassi took over two months off before returning to an event in San Jose in February where he reached the semfinals. But since then Agassi has failed to win a match in four attempts. Talent alone kept him alive in the first set with 79th-ranked Draper which he narrowly lost when he missed a backhand in the tiebreaker.

After that Agassi's timing fell apart as Draper grabbed a 4-1 second set lead. Agassi missed two chances to break the Australian in the sixth game and get back into the match. Instead, trailing 1-5, he dropped serve at love to give Draper the 6-1 victory with another errant backhand deep.

"It's obvious I have some hurdles to overcome," Agassi said. "I'm still second-guessing my shot selection. It should be instinctive. I wish I believed in myself out there as much as people believe in my ability. When I'm expecting to win I'm a different player."

Draper said he went on court with a carefree attitude to "just try to enjoy myself and not get too stressed. I knew Andre had been struggling with his confidence and a lot of guys have been beating him so I gave myself a chance to win. I was trying to play and not think of the outcome that I was beating Andre Agassi."
Becker was replaced in the field by Lucas Arnold of Argentina, a lucky loser from the qualifying competition.

"I wanted to wait until the last minute for some improvements which didn't come," said Becker, who has played in only one tournament this year in Dubai, where he withdrew with the same wrist trouble after advancing to the quarterfinals.
"I decided that I'm not ready yet for a match. But time is going to be the healer. The injury is basically gone, but I'm not strong enough yet in my wrist."
Becker is Miami's newest celebrity resident with a second home purchased recently on nearby Fisher Island. But his history with the city's tennis tournament has been patchy.

In 1987 he pulled out, citing food poisoning. In 1993 he got a second-round walkover when his opponent, Gianluca Pozzi, suffered appendicitis. He then gave his third-round opponent, Nicklas Kulti of Sweden, a walkover of his own.

In 1994 Becker was enduring such a drubbing from Andre Agassi in their third-round match that he handed his racquet to local ballgirl, Stephanie Flaherty, who won him a point. Agassi still won the match 6-2 7-5. Becker's best result at the tournament was in '92 when he reached the fourth round.
Becker denied that he is about to make Miami his primary residence. German tax authorities raided his home in December and his interracial marriage has been the target of threats.

"It's simply wrong," said Becker of the rumours of a permanent move to the United States. "I'm still a German taxpayer. This is my holiday home. But it's going to be probably a court battle sooner or later. I cannot talk anything more specific about the case."
